analysis.one_liner: Requires giant social media and messaging platforms to let users take their data and connect across competing apps.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill by five senators to force the largest online platforms to open up their networks never received a committee vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted online platforms with more than 100 million U.S. users that make money from people's data. It would have required those platforms to let users export their data to a competitor, to interoperate — meaning a user of one app could communicate directly with a user of another — and to let users appoint a third-party agent to manage their accounts. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the rules, and violating them could bring fines counted per affected user. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Users of the largest social media and messaging services, who could leave a platform without losing their photos, contacts, and message history, and could reach people on other apps without everyone using the same service. Smaller and would-be competitors also gain, because the biggest advantage of the giant platforms — the network of people you already know there — becomes something they can plug into instead of having to rebuild.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of major social and messaging platforms

how_it_helps.text: Platforms with over 100 million U.S. users must provide interfaces so users can transfer their data to themselves or to a competing service in a machine-readable format [S2].

Platforms must maintain interoperability interfaces on fair, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory terms so users of competing services can communicate with their users, and changes made to undermine that access count as violations [S2].

Users may designate a registered third-party agent to manage their account, content, and settings on their behalf, with the agent barred from using the user's data for its own commercial benefit [S2].

The FTC enforces the Act and, in assessing fines, must count each affected user as a separate violation, which makes violations of a service with hundreds of millions of users enormously expensive [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The large platform companies themselves, which would lose a major advantage: the difficulty of switching that keeps users on their services. They would bear the cost of building and maintaining the required interfaces, and they could face per-user fines. Some compliance costs and any access fees the platforms are allowed to charge could ultimately show up in the price of services users pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large platform companies like Meta and Google

drawbacks.text: Opening platform networks through third-party-accessible interfaces creates new security and privacy risks: competing providers and delegated agents that access user data could be breached or misused, which is why the bill requires those parties to secure the data and lets the FTC deregister agents that violate their duties [S2].

Interoperability between messaging networks can make spam, scams, and unwanted content easier to spread across services, and the bill allows platforms to set security and privacy standards for access in response to such threats [S2].

The rules are technically demanding and the effective date is tied to the FTC finishing its regulations, so compliance costs and the platform's ability to charge fees proportional to the cost and risk of providing access could be passed along or used to slow competitors [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: today a person's social graph and content are effectively held hostage by the platform they joined, and this bill attacks that lock-in directly, the way number portability did for phone numbers. The costs are genuine but manageable — security risks that the bill tries to contain through registration, standards, and FTC enforcement, and compliance burdens that fall on companies with more than 100 million users. The bill would not directly lower prices or raise wages, but it would give ordinary users something they largely lack today: a real exit option.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by a bipartisan group of five senators and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in July 2023, and the committee never acted on it; the bill died there when that Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Warner introduced the ACCESS Act on July 26, 2023, joined by Senators Blumenthal and Klobuchar, both Democrats, and Graham and Hawley, both Republicans [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, through the end of the 118th Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large platform companies, which keep the network lock-in the bill would have removed, and the committee leadership that never had to take a position on it.

for.name: Sen. Mark Warner
for.role: U.S. Senator from Virginia, lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and authored its portability, interoperability, and delegability requirements.

for.name: Sens. Blumenthal, Klobuchar (D) and Graham, Hawley (R)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from both parties at introduction.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill during the entire Congress.

against.name: Major social media and messaging platforms
against.role: Companies with more than 100 million U.S. users that the bill would regulate
against.what_they_did: Opposed interoperability and portability mandates that would erode the switching costs protecting their user bases.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship from the start — three senators from the Democratic caucus and two Republicans — and died in committee without any vote, so no roll calls exist to measure the split.

industries.industry: Large social media and messaging platforms (Meta, Google, and similar companies)
industries.note: These companies profit from the difficulty of leaving their services; the bill would force them to build data portability, interoperability, and account-delegation interfaces and face per-user fines for violations. Their gain from the bill's failure is the public's loss of exit options.

Startups and smaller apps could plug into the large platforms' networks and attract users with their data intact, rather than having to rebuild a social network from zero. This only works if a user can leave, which is why it runs alongside users' interests.
The bill covers platforms that earn income from collecting, processing, selling, or sharing user data, and would loosen their grip on that data by letting users move it elsewhere.

A new class of FTC-registered agents that would manage users' accounts for a fee, creating a business opportunity regulated by the FTC — a convenience for users that also adds a party holding their data.
